unit.title: Flourishing and detachment
unit.needIt: This helps you stay calm when things go wrong. You can learn to stop worrying about things you cannot change, like the weather or other people's moods.
unit.why: Epictetus was a slave who learned to find inner peace by focusing only on his own choices. He taught that we suffer because we try to control the world instead of our own minds.
unit.outcome: Distinguish between what you can control and what you cannot.

quiz.q: What was Epictetus's early life like?
quiz.why: The lecture states he spent a significant portion of his life as a slave.
quiz.quote: He spent the early portion of his life as a slave.

quiz.q: What is the Stoic view of the world?
quiz.why: Stoics believed the world is an organic totality governed by divine reason.
quiz.quote: So Stoics held with respect to the underlying metaphysical about reality, that the world itself is an organic physical totality that's governed by what they called logos or divine reason.

quiz.q: What is the 'mistake' Epictetus warns about?
choices: Confusing what is ours with what is not
quiz.why: He says confusing what we can control with what we cannot leads to misery.
quiz.quote: The mistake of confusing that over which you have control and that over which you lack control leads to thwarted, upset, miserable, blamingness.

quiz.q: How does Epictetus describe the role of judgment?
quiz.why: He argues that things are not good or bad on their own; our judgment gives them that meaning.
quiz.quote: It is your assessment of the event that gives it that valence.

quiz.q: What does Epictetus say we should do with our desires?
quiz.why: He suggests we should want things to happen as they do happen.
quiz.quote: Do not want to have events happen to you as you want them to, but instead want them to happen as they do happen.

quiz.q: What is the 'direction of fit' example used in the lecture?
quiz.why: The lecture uses a shopping list to show how shaping desires to fit the world prevents frustration.
quiz.quote: So because I had some parchment left over from that contract that we signed with the devil a few weeks ago, I thought I'd use it for my shopping list.

quiz.q: What did Stockdale say was the most harmful thing?
quiz.why: Stockdale felt that destroying his internal character was the greatest harm.
quiz.quote: Epictetus, look not for any greater harm than this, destroying the trustworthy, self-respecting, well-behaved man inside you.

crystal.key: True flourishing comes from distinguishing what is within your power from what is not.

decoys.why: The lecture says it is about acting in accord with reason, not just suppressing emotion.

decoys.text: Epictetus believed social ties don't matter.
decoys.why: Stockdale's story shows that human connection is still very important.

crystal.aha: By narrowing your focus to your own will, you become invincible to external misfortune.
